title: Purpose, audience, and context
keyIdea: Before you judge a text, ask three questions. Purpose: what does the writer want the reader to think or do? Audience: who is it written for? Context: when, where and why was it written? The answers explain the writer's choices of register, tone, vocabulary and structure. The same fact is written differently for scientists, newspaper readers and young children.
familyTip: Pick one news story and find it in two places, such as a tabloid front page and a science website or a children's news site. Ask: who is each one for, and which words show it? What does each writer want you to feel or do?

visual.caption: Who is each sentence written for? Drag each card to its most likely reader, or tap the card then a box.

items: Samples were analysed using infrared spectroscopy.

SCANDAL! Beach left buried in plastic
Experts warn that our seas are in trouble.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: match one fact to three readers, tap report conventions, rewrite it for two readers, find a primary purpose and read a 1912 text in context.

kid: Every text is written for someone, for a reason, at a time. Purpose is what the writer wants you to think or do. Audience is who it is for. Context is when, where and why it was made.
One fact can be written in many ways. A report says microplastics were found in 94% of samples. A paper shouts PLASTIC PERIL! A book for small children says little bits of plastic get into the sea.

To find the audience, look at the words, not the topic. Reports use exact numbers and careful words like suggest. Headlines use capitals and shock words. Books for small children use short, easy sentences.

A text can have two purposes. A charity leaflet gives facts, but its main aim is to get you to give money. Context counts too. In 1912, a paper called the Titanic unsinkable. It was written before the ship sank.
adult: Ages 11 to 14. National Curriculum in England, Key Stage 3 English: pupils read critically, knowing how language, vocabulary choice, grammar and text structure present meaning, and they study texts from different times. In the US Common Core, RI.6.6 to RI.8.6 ask students to find an author's purpose and point of view and how it shapes the text.

Purpose, audience and context work together. The audience sets the register (formal or informal), the vocabulary (technical or everyday) and the conventions of the form. The purpose explains what the text asks the reader to do. The context, such as the date, place and publisher, explains what the writer and first readers knew and believed.

Common mistakes: judging the audience by the topic instead of the language (a text about dinosaurs is not always for children); thinking a text full of facts must only inform, when the facts may serve a call to action; reading hedging words such as suggest as weakness rather than scientific care; and judging an old text by what we know now instead of its context.

In the lab your teenager matches three versions of one microplastics fact to their readers, taps five conventions of a science report, rewrites the fact for a picture book and a journal, finds the line that reveals a charity leaflet's primary purpose, places a 1912 Titanic clipping on a timeline, and names the purpose, audience and context of a school letter.

practice.prompt: “Isotopic evidence indicates an asteroid impact 66 million years ago.” Who is the most likely audience?
choices: Young children, because it is about dinosaurs
Teen readers of a gaming site
practice.hint: Look at the words, not the topic. Would a child know “isotopic”?
practice.explain: “Isotopic evidence” and “indicates” are technical, careful words for experts. The topic alone does not decide the audience.

practice.prompt: A report tested {n} samples and found microplastics in all but {k} of them. How many samples contained microplastics?
practice.hint: Take the samples without microplastics away from the total.
practice.explain: {n} − {k} = {=n-k} samples. A report gives exact numbers like this; a headline might only say “almost every sample”.

practice.prompt: A leaflet lists facts about plastic, then ends: “Give £5 today.” What is its primary purpose?
choices: To inform, because it is mostly facts
practice.hint: What does the writer want the reader to do at the end?
practice.explain: The facts build up to a call to action. Informing is a secondary purpose; persuading is the primary one.

practice.prompt: A newspaper wrote about the Titanic on {d} April 1912. The ship sank on 15 April. How many days before the sinking was it written?
practice.hint: Take the date of writing away from 15.
practice.explain: 15 − {d} = {=15-d} days. The writer could not know what would happen, which is part of the text's context.

practice.prompt: Why might a scientist write “the results suggest” instead of “the results prove”?
choices: To say exactly how far the evidence goes
Because they do not understand the topic
practice.hint: Scientists are careful not to claim more than their data shows.
practice.explain: This is hedging, a convention of scientific writing. It signals care about evidence, not ignorance.

pool.prompt: “Yo! School disco Friday 🎉 Wear something sparkly!!” Who is the audience?
pool.hint: Look at the register: how chatty is it?
pool.explain: “Yo!”, the emoji and “!!” are informal and chatty, which suits pupils. A letter to parents would be formal.

pool.prompt: “Dear Parents and Carers, the Year 8 trip is on Friday. Please return the consent form by Monday.” Who is the audience?
pool.hint: Who does the letter speak to in its first words?
pool.explain: The letter is about Year 8, but “Dear Parents and Carers” names the readers. The topic and the audience are different things.

pool.prompt: Which feature is a convention of a science report rather than a newspaper?
choices: Stating the sample size, such as n = 120
pool.hint: Which one helps an expert judge the evidence?
pool.explain: A sample size lets experts judge how reliable a result is. Capitals and shock words are headline conventions for a general reader.

pool.prompt: A 1912 newspaper calls the Titanic “practically unsinkable”. What is the best way to read this?
choices: In its context: it was written before the ship sank
As a lie, because we know it sank
pool.hint: What did the writer and readers know on that date?
pool.explain: Before 15 April 1912 many people believed the ship was very safe. Reading in context means judging by what was known then.

pool.prompt: A writer turns a science fact into a picture book for 6-year-olds. What should change?
choices: The words and tone, not the fact
The fact, to make it simpler but untrue
pool.hint: Can a fact be explained simply and still be true?
pool.explain: Register and vocabulary change with the audience: “little bits of plastic” instead of “microplastic particles”. The fact stays true.

pool.prompt: “SHOCK AS TINY PLASTIC FOUND IN 94% OF SAMPLES”. Why the capitals and “SHOCK”?
choices: To grab a general reader's attention
pool.hint: Where would you see a line like this, and who is it trying to catch?
pool.explain: Capitals and shock words are headline conventions to catch a general reader's eye. The exact data is the 94%.

pool.prompt: A text was published in {y}. How many years ago was that from 2026?
pool.hint: Subtract the year it was written from 2026.
pool.explain: 2026 − {y} = {=2026-y} years. Knowing how old a text is helps you think about its context: what people knew and believed then.

pool.prompt: “Please do not touch the exhibits. Flash photography is not permitted.” What is the primary purpose?
pool.hint: Is the sign telling you something to do or not do?
pool.explain: Imperatives such as “do not touch” instruct the reader. The formal register suits a public sign.

pool.prompt: A leaflet has {f} sentences of facts and 1 sentence asking you to donate. How many sentences does it have in total?
pool.hint: Add the fact sentences and the one call to action.
pool.explain: {f} + 1 = {=f+1} sentences. Even with only 1 call to action among {=f+1} sentences, persuading is the primary purpose: the facts lead up to it.
